answer.rationale: Primary objective is to minimize TCO without increasing delivery risk. Finance mandates an 18% spend cut; contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew; assembly line has no buffer, so any supplier switch or second-source onboarding adds delivery risk we cannot absorb. The primary path that addresses cost pressure without moving supply is to renegotiate terms with the incumbent at renewal. Memory_c4 (day 29) supports that benchmarking at renewal has historically recovered real margin on both price and payment terms. Memory_c1 (day 21) supports that staying with the incumbent preserves integration stability with zero migration or interruption. Memory_c6 (day 65) is the one I choose to verify because it suggests a multi-year commitment with the incumbent unlocks volume pricing—exactly the lever needed to meet an 18% cut without narrowing scope. If the archived record confirms that the longer term genuinely reduced unit cost and did not narrow service scope, a multi-year renegotiation is the highest-confidence move. Switching vendors (memory_c2) saves cost but adds onboarding risk at zero buffer. Adding a second source (memory_c3) helps resilience but not cost, and exceeds our one-decision capacity alongside the renewal. Deferring (memory_c5) is viable for non-critical renewals, but this is the primary supply contract feeding an assembly line at 94% capacity, so deferral risks a lapse and is not acceptable. Therefore: negotiate a multi-year renewal with the incumbent, benchmarked against market rates, targeting the 18% reduction through volume pricing and improved payment terms.
